analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate tax exemption in half and spends part of the added revenue on child care grants.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with zero cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and has seen no action since; Congress is still in session.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Early Childhood Education Trust Fund funded by 15% of estate tax receipts each year [S2]. To raise that revenue, it would cut the estate tax exemption from $15 million to $7 million for estates of people dying after December 31, 2025, meaning more large estates would owe the tax [S2]. The fund would pay for new child care supply grants to state agencies under the existing Child Care and Development Block Grant program [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Families who need child care and child care providers, who would receive new federal grant money routed through the existing child care block grant system [S2]. The federal government also gains revenue from estates above the lower exemption, which would pay tax at rates that reach 40% on the largest amounts.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated trust fund, with 15% of annual estate tax receipts appropriated to it automatically each year [S2].

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to award child care supply grants to each state's lead agency under section 658O of the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act, adding to existing block grant funding rather than replacing it [S2].
Lowers the estate tax exemption from $15 million to $7 million, so estates between those values become taxable and estates above $7 million owe more [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Heirs of estates valued above $7 million, who would face the federal estate tax on amounts between $7 million and the current $15 million exemption, taxed at rates up to 40%.

drawbacks.text: The exemption cut applies to all estates over $7 million, including family-owned farms and businesses that are asset-rich but cash-poor, which can face pressure to sell assets to pay the tax — the standard objection to lowering the exemption.

The grant language waives several requirements of the existing child care block grant law, including certain rules in section 658E(c)(3) and section 658G, trading some of the program's existing protections and priorities for flexibility [S2].
15% of estate tax receipts is a small share of a tax paid by relatively few estates, so the new child care money would be modest compared with the cost of care for most families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is direct and legible: a meaningful tax increase on the largest estates funds new child care grants on top of existing block grant funding. The main design weaknesses are the small size of the funding stream and the waiver of some existing block grant requirements. The political obstacle is not design but the fact that the majority party has moved in the opposite direction on the estate tax.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce committees in July 2025 and neither has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; with zero cosponsors and Congress still in session, it sits untouched in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Sara Jacobs introduced the bill in the House on July 10, 2025 [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Education and Workforce [S4].
No member from either party has cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero [S3].
No action beyond the referral appears in the bill's action history — no hearing, markup, subcommittee referral, or vote has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the status quo prevails: heirs of estates above the current exemption keep the $15 million exclusion, and no new child care funding is created. The people better off under the outcome so far are those who would have paid the higher estate tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Heirs of large estates keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so there is no roll-call split to report; the bill has one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and the committee chairs who would move it are Republicans.

industries.industry: Heirs of large estates and high-net-worth households
industries.note: Cutting the exemption from $15 million to $7 million would newly tax estates between those values and increase the bill for larger ones, at rates reaching 40%. The benefit to ordinary people — child care funding — comes directly from that revenue.

New supply grants would flow to state lead agencies under the existing block grant system, adding money on top of current funding. Providers' interest in this bill runs alongside families' need for care.

analysis.trajectory: Most House bills die in committee, and the odds here are especially poor: zero cosponsors, no committee movement in months, a House majority that has acted to keep the estate tax exemption high, and an automatic revenue mechanism requiring no annual vote. Absent unusual bipartisan interest, expect the bill to expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
